In the second step, the optimal bin size (.025-s, to preview the results) was carried forward to train a final classifier on all of the odd trials from each condition and test the classifier on the remaining data (even trials from each condition).

For the last type of analyses, we sought to further characterize the time course and frequency bands that were driving the classifications. These analyses made further use of the data binned into .025-s segments, but instead of using time merely as a feature, tracked classifier performance for the ERP and oscillatory patterns in two ways. The time courses of neural differences were constructed for ERP and oscillatory patterns in parallel by cycling the classification procedure across successive time bins. To additionally characterize the frequency bands involved in classifying oscillatory activity, the classification procedure was cycled over each combination of time (.025-s bins) and frequency (in 1-Hz increments). Due to the number of separate classifications required for these analyses, we took the approach involved in the final classification of time (as described above), where individual classifiers were trained on the odd trials from each condition and tested on the even trials from each condition (i.e., k-fold cross-validation was not implemented).

For all analyses involving multiple statistical tests across non-independent data points, cluster-based Monte Carlo simulations were implemented to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007). For the time course analyses, individual cluster-wise statistics correspond to the summed t-values (hereafter, tsum) over clustered (i.e., consecutively significant) time points (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007). For the time-frequency analyses, cluster-wise statistics (tsum) were determined across both the time and frequency dimensions. Each simulation involved 1000 randomly-shuffled permutations of the condition labels. The alpha level for individual data points was set to .05 and, as with the previous analyses of AUC, the group-level statistical tests were one-tailed against the chance level of .5. The resulting p-values reported in the Results (see section 3.2.) correspond to the proportion of larger clusters (based on tsum) from the permutation-based null distribution.

To summarize the individual features contributing to the foregoing classifications, the trained classifier weights were extracted. Our implementation of LDA results in a single weight value associated with each feature (also see Blankertz et al., 2011; Treder, 2020). To allow for description of the sign and magnitude of the weights at the group level, each subject's weights were standardized into t-values (vs. a weight of 0). We emphasize that the resulting weights are presented here purely for descriptive purposes for two reasons. First, similarity across subjects in feature values is not a requirement for classification success. That is, each subject's data were classified independently given that there might be variation in how subjects differentially process the forward and backward conditions. Second, there is no need for the weights of adjacent features (e.g., nearby electrodes for ERP data, or nearby electrodes or frequency bands for the oscillatory data) to be correlated. Therefore, we did not apply any cluster-correction procedures to these descriptive results.

3. RESULTS

>RESULTS >Behavioral performance

3.1.1. Overall recall accuracy

Analysis of the behavioral data first assessed overall performance on the cued recall task. Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure 1a). If both words could not be recalled, subjects were to report partial information or make their best guess, with the instructions emphasizing the report of words from the cued direction (which was most relevant to the EEG classification analyses). As shown in Figure 2b, against the ideal of two words reported per list, the average number of all words reported differed significantly at 2.25 (SD = .46; t23 = 2.65, p = .014).

The behavioral data were next segregated according to accuracy. Although there are numerous ways to consider recall accuracy, we took an approach here focusing on the instructional emphasis of whether words were correctly reported from the cued direction (i.e., previous words in the list for backward recall and subsequent words in the list for forward recall), regardless of the strict order of report or adherence to only the two words directly adjacent to the cue. For example, if cued with the word from the third list position and in the forward direction, whereas the ideal response would be the fourth and then fifth words, our criterion for being correct also included reporting the fifth then fourth words, as well as reporting the fifth then seventh words. Figure 1a provides some additional examples of possible responses and their corresponding condition labels. Recall performance according to whether words were reported from the cued (correct) direction, from the uncued (incorrect) direction, or not from the current list at all (i.e., extra-list intrusions) is summarized in Figure 1b. As is apparent, words from the cued direction (M = 1.64, SD = 0.39) considerably exceeded those from the uncued direction (M = 0.26, SD = 0.15) and intrusions (M = 0.30, SD = 0.22).

To statistically test whether performance differed across the accuracy categories described above or with respect to the experimental manipulations, the measures were submitted to a three-way ANOVA including factors of accuracy category (cued direction, uncued direction, or intrusion), recall direction (forward or backward), and study list length (7, 8, or 9 words). As expected, there was a significant main effect of accuracy category (F1.41,32.35 = 193.90, p < .001; fractional dfs correspond to Greenhouse-Geisser correction), with recall in the cued direction exceeding both that in the uncued direction (t23 = 14.48, p < .001) and intrusions (t23 = 15.25, p < .001), whereas the latter two categories did not differ (t23 = .67, p = .51). Given the importance of equating the forward and backward conditions (see Introduction), Figure 1c provides the measures for each accuracy category according to this distinction. As is apparent from the figure, responding was comparable for forward and backward recall, with the ANOVA revealing no significant effects involving the recall direction factor (all Fs < 1, except the recall direction × list length interaction, F1.61,37.12 = 2.75, p = .087). Additionally, no other significant effects involving the list length or accuracy category factors were observed (all Fs < 1, except the accuracy category × list length interaction, F2.37,54.43 = 1.39, p = .26).

3.1.2. Position and lag effects

To further facilitate comparison of performance in our directional cued recall task with the findings of other investigations of directional retrieval, the behavioral data were next examined with respect to serial position and lag effects. Figure 2 displays the proportions of correctly reporting a word from a particular serial position, given that the position was one of the two cued for subjects to report, separated by recall direction and list length. To test for any systematic effects across serial position, we simplified the list length manipulation by collapsing positions into three bins-early (first two positions), late (last two positions), and middle (the remaining positions, which differed according to list length)-as is shown in Figure 2d. A two-way ANOVA then probed effects of recall direction (forward or backward) and position bin (early, middle, or late), revealing only a significant main effect of position bin (F1.68,38.53 = 4.00, p = .033). Although accuracy did not differ between the early and late bins (t23 = .11, p = .91), accuracy for the middle bin was significantly lower than that for the other two (respectively, t23 = 2.78 and 2.76, both ps = .011). Importantly, consistent with our previous results for the different accuracy categories, there were again no significant effects involving the recall direction factor (main effect: F < 1; interaction: F1.76,40.42 = 1.88, p = .17). Effects of lag were assessed in the form of lag-related conditional response probabilities (CRPs; Kahana, 1996), which are displayed in Figure 3. As was shown for the earlier analyses, these plots also indicated that more recalls occur in the cued as opposed to uncued direction. Additionally, words closer to the cued position were appropriately recalled more often than those from farther positions (indicating subject compliance with the instructions), and these effects appeared to be preserved across list length. As was done for the serial position analysis, we collapsed the data over list length by binning the original lags into three bins (see Figure 3d): near (adjacent two positions), middle (next two positions), and far (remaining positions, which again differed with list length). A three-way ANOVA with factors of accuracy category (cued or uncued; note the removal of intrusions given the absence of lag information), recall direction (forward or backward), and lag (near, middle, or far), revealed significant main effects of accuracy category (F1,23 = 457.65, p < .001) and lag (F1.34,30.80 = 75.17, p < .001), as well as an interaction between these two variables (F1.32,30.254 = 19.19, p < .001). In addition to recalls being more frequent in the cued than uncued direction, and performance being better for nearer positions, the decline in performance with increasing lag was greater for responses in the cued (correct) direction. As before, there were no significant effects involving the recall direction factor (recall direction × lag bin: F1.53,35.07 = 1.33, p = .27; three-way interaction: F1.64,37.79 = 1.12, p = .33; other Fs < 1). Together with the results of the previous analyses, the overall absence of behavioral differences between the forward and backward conditions allows for attributing any further neural distinction to recall direction instead of to other, confounding differences across conditions (e.g., effort, difficulty, or success).

3.2. EEG classification

The primary goal of the EEG classification analyses was to determine whether patterns of neural activity could provide novel evidence that retrieval deliberation and search were distinguishable between the forward versus backward directions. To this end, the EEG was classified in a series of analyses that used, in parallel, either ERP (voltage) amplitude or oscillatory (spectral) power. First, we collapsed these data across the entire retrieval cue deliberation period, under the assumption that processing in service of retrieval direction was continually maintained during this time. Next, in case differential processing varied across time (as opposed to being engaged consistently), the analyses turned to including time as an additional classification feature. Finally, we cycled the classification procedure across specific time bins and frequency bands, allowing for characterization of features in the EEG data that could potentially inform subsequent research on directional retrieval processing while also ensuring the reliability of our effects according to cluster-based statistical correction.

3.2.1. Overall classification irrespective of time

Given that subjects were instructed to deliberate about retrieval throughout the 5-s period in which the word and direction cues were presented, the classification analyses were initially conducted on the EEG data averaged over this period. While classified ERP patterns consisted of 60 features (voltage amplitude at each electrode), oscillatory patterns comprised 7,020 features (spectral power from 4 to 120 Hz in 1-Hz increments × 60 electrodes). As shown in Figure 4a, mean performance (AUC) of the resulting ERP classifier was numerically below chance at .48 (SD = .082; t23 = -1.41, p = .91). (Note that one-tailed statistical tests were used when contrasting AUC against chance, given the alternative hypothesis that any discriminable information between conditions should increase classifier performance.) Despite the forward and backward conditions being indistinguishable based on averaged ERP data, classifying the oscillatory data resulted in a mean AUC of .54 (SD = .097; also see Figure 4a), which significantly exceeded the chance level (t23 = 2.26, p = .017). Directly comparing the performance of the ERP-and oscillation-based classifiers also revealed a significant difference (t23 = 2.27, p = .033).

3.2.2. Classification with time as a feature

The preceding analyses indicated that classifying the EEG data collapsed over time, while giving rise to significant above-chance performance for the oscillatory data, still resulted in accuracy levels that were near or below chance for several subjects. One possible reason for this limit on observed classification performance is that, rather than being engaged consistently throughout the 5-s deliberation period, the neural processes differentiating the forward and backward conditions fluctuated across time. The next analyses thus examined whether time carried information important to retrieval direction by including it as an additional classification feature.

Using time as a feature involved a two-step approach in which an optimal time bin size was first selected via cross-validation on half of the data and then a final classifier was evaluated on the remaining, untouched half of the data (see section 2.5. for further details). Figure 4b summarizes the results of the first step for the ERP and oscillatory data across a range of bin sizes: 5, 2.5, 1, .5, .25, .1, .05, and .025 s. As shown, AUC for the ERP classification was numerically below chance for the largest bin (5 s: M = .47, SD = .17, t23 = -.78, p = .78) with performance increasing to about .55 by the .5-s bin (M = .55, SD = .17, t23 = 1.50, p = .074) and then leveling off for the remaining shorter ones (for .025-s: M = .55, SD = .16, t23 = 1.64, p = .057). For the oscillatory classification, the results were less clear, with AUC values overall being closer to chance and having a maximum value of .51 (SD = .13, t23 = .40, p = .35) at the .025-s bin size. Note that it is unsurprising that performance for the previous classifications (see Figure 4a) is less noisy than that reported here when time is a feature, since the latter is based on classifying only half of the available data (odd trials from each condition).

However, the present results do indicate that the shortest time bin is optimal for ERP data and equally as good as the longer bins for oscillatory data.

Carrying forward the .025-s bin size to the final analyses resulted in classifying electrode × time patterns of 12,000 features (60 electrodes × 200 time bins) for the ERP data and electrode × frequency × time patterns of about 1.4 million features (60 electrodes × 117 frequencies × 200 time bins) for the oscillatory data. As displayed in Figure 4a, the ERP classification gave rise to performance (M = .52, SD = .14) that was numerically above chance, in contrast to the below-chance results found in the initial (collapsed) analysis, but this was still not significantly greater than the chance level (t23 = .88, p = .19). Performance for the oscillatory classifier, though, again significantly exceeded chance (M = .57, SD = .12, t23 = 2.79, p = .0052), consistent with the results from collapsing over time. Directly comparing the ERP and oscillatory results failed to result in a significant difference (t23 = 1.13, p = .27), presumably due to the increase in ERP performance.

3.2.3. Time-and frequency-specific classifier features

In the final set of analyses, we sought to characterize the time course and frequency signature of forward vs. backward retrieval, under the assumption that differential processing might be engaged in a more transient manner as opposed to sustained across the entire deliberation period. As displayed in Figures 5a and 5b, classification performance for the ERP and oscillatory data, respectively, was fairly variable across time. To test for the presence of any statistically reliable effects, a simulation-based correction procedure for multiple comparisons was employed over consecutive significant time bins (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007; also see section 2.5.). For the ERP data, there were 15 individually-significant time bins, five of which formed clusters of at least two consecutive bins. Of these clusters, none surpassed the cluster-wise corrected threshold (at the .05 alpha level, one-tailed), with the cluster exhibiting the maximum statistic taking place over only three bins (2.625 to 2.675 s; tsum = 6.49; p = .14; Figure 5a). For the oscillatory data, classification gave rise to 22 individually-significant time points that were clustered into seven contiguous groups. Of these, two clusters exceeded the significance threshold, as shown in Figure 5b: an early one at .75 to .825 s after cue onset (four bins; tsum = 11.01, p = .0060) and a later one at 2.325 to 2.45 s (six bins; tsum = 14.72, p = .0010). 825 s (early) and from 2.325 to 2.450 s (late), that were significant according to the cluster-wise correction procedure. (c) Scalp topography maps of the trained classifier weights for the significant early and late clusters from the previous panel. The weights were transformed into t-values and collapsed into five frequency bands (theta, 4-8 Hz; alpha, 9-12 Hz; beta, 13-30 Hz; low gamma, 31-70 Hz; and high gamma, 71-120 Hz). Asterisks indicate positive and negative weights that passed a standard threshold (t23 = ±2.069, p < .05). Note that these maps are intended to be used solely for descriptive purposes.

Figure 5c displays the scalp topographies of t-transformed trained weights for the significant clusters of time bins identified from the classification of oscillatory activity. As described in the Methods (section 2.5.), our use of t-values here is purely descriptive and not intended for statistical inference. To simplify the results, the weight maps were collapsed into five traditional frequency bands: theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (9-12 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), low gamma (31-70 Hz), and high gamma (71-120 Hz). Additionally, to highlight the electrodes and frequency bands exhibiting the strongest weights, a standard, critical t-value (t23 = 2.069, p < .05, two-tailed) was used for thresholding. As shown in the figure, notable electrode-wise weight values for the early cluster were evident in the alpha band (F8 and CP3: t23 = -2.26 and -2.49), low gamma band (Fp1 and F7: t23 = -2.09 and -2.32), and high gamma band (F6: t23 = -2.25). For the late cluster, threshold-exceeding weights were observed in beta band (P1: t23 = 2.35) and high gamma band (T8, P8, PO7, and FC4: t23 = 2.43, 2.18, 2.14, and -2.12). The statistical reliability of these effects was further explored in the next analysis.

To test whether the time-resolved differences described above were restricted to particular oscillatory frequencies, individual classifications were conducted on the electrode-wise activity patterns for each time (.025-s bins) × frequency (in 1-Hz increments) combination. The time-frequency plots of resulting AUC values are displayed in Figure 6a. Analogous to the previous analyses, a multiple-comparisons correction procedure was used to provide cluster-wise statistics across both the time and frequency dimensions. Although there were several (34 to be exact) clusters of at least two individually-significant data points (at an alpha level of .05, onetailed), only one of these clusters was significant according to the correction procedure. As shown in Figure 6b, the significant cluster (tsum = 242.17, p = .020) consisted of 114 data points, extending from 48 to 102 Hz and from 2.35 to 2.475 s (overlapping with the latency from the previous analyses, as shown in Figure 5b). To further describe the classifier results for this significant cluster, Figure 6c displays the topographic map of electrode-wise weight values, which indicated that the strongest weights were at electrodes F5 and T8 (t23 = 2.14 and 2.88, respectively). Due to this cluster partially overlapping with two of our pre-experimentallydefined frequency bands, the scalp maps of trained classifier weights are also provided separately according to the boundary between the low and high gamma bands. As shown in the figure, the strongest weights for rightlateralized temporal and parietal electrodes are present for both bands (for low gamma, T8 and TP8: t23 = 2.39 and 2.57; for high gamma, T8 and P8: t23 = 2.68 and 2.29). The lower band additionally exhibited strong positive weights at electrodes T7 and O1 (t23 = 2.31 and 2.28, respectively), whereas the higher band was associated with a strong positive weight at PO7 (t23 = 2.09) and a strong negative weight at F2 (t23 = -2.27).

4. DISCUSSION

As described in the Introduction (see section 1.), numerous studies using different list-memory paradigms have shown that the temporal sequence of events during memory encoding can influence how those events are later retrieved. The underlying neural correlates of retrieving sequences of memories, and in particular whether forward and backward retrieval processes can be neurally distinguished, remain to be elucidated, in part due to consistent evidence that backward retrieval search is considerably less frequent and is usually associated with worse behavioral performance than forward search (e.g., Guitard et al., 2020 Guitard et al., , 2022;; Kahana, 1996; Kahana and Caplan, 2002; Murdock, 1968; but see Madigan, 1971). Here, we employed an experimental procedure that attempted to equate behavior across retrieval direction so that EEG data could be used to characterize any differences in neural processing. After studying lists of about eight successively presented words, subjects undertook an immediate, directional cued recall task in which they were instructed to recall two list words by moving either forward or backward relative to the provided cue. The behavioral results indicated success of the task's primary goal, in that subjects were able to report the desired number of recalled items. Additionally, across both the forward and backward conditions, correct recall in the cued direction substantially exceeded incorrect recall in the uncued direction as well as the report of extra-list intrusions.

Our behavioral results further aligned with findings widely observed in the literature on list memory. Namely, we found differences in behavioral accuracy according to serial position, where performance was better for words from the early and late list positions compared to those from the middle (see Figure 2). These findings are consistent with serial position effects that have been shown in both serial and free recall tasks (e.g., Deese and Kaufman, 1957; Howard and Kahana, 1999; Jahnke, 1965; Murdock, 1962; Ward et al., 2010). Additionally, lag-based analyses of our cued recall data, employing the conditional response probability (CRP) measure routinely used in studies of free recall (e.g., Kahana, 1996; for review, see Healey et al., 2019; but see Farrell and Lewandowsky, 2008, for limitations), revealed that words nearer to the cued position were recalled at higher rates than those more distant. Importantly, considering the current results in the context of these position and lag effects indicated that subjects were able to successfully retrieve memories in both directions and, moreover, did so with equivalent performance across direction. Taken together, these behavioral findings meet the prerequisite to be able to use the corresponding EEG data to distinguish brain activity on the basis of potentially qualitatively-distinct directional retrieval processes as opposed to being conflated by other, generally less interesting factors such as task difficulty, effort, or whether the outcome of the retrieval search was successful.

Turning to the EEG findings, our use of MVPA was able to sensitively detect neural activity patterns that differed between the forward and backward conditions and were presumably a reflection of the distinct deliberation and search processes that served the two directions of recall. This approach was largely exploratory given the lack of existing studies that contrasted directional retrieval in list-learning paradigms, particular with EEG (cf. Hoshi et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2005). Borrowing from recent studies employing scalp EEG to investigate neural activity just prior to verbal report in free recall tasks (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024), our analyses focused on a 5-second period that preceded recall vocalization, allowing for assessment of retrieval-related processes while minimizing artifacts in the EEG due to vocalization. Additionally, our cued recall procedure ensured adequate numbers of trials per directional retrieval condition to allow for balanced classifier training, contrasting with the imbalance between forward and backward list transitions often observed in free recall. To this end, the present analyses produced multiple results differentiating the two conditions, some of which are highlighted here for further discussion.

First, parallel analyses directed at classifying ERP amplitude and oscillatory activity demonstrated that only the latter consistently gave rise to accuracy levels that significantly exceeded chance (but see, e.g., Carlson et al., 2011, and Johnson et al., 2015, for positive results with ERP data). This difference according to data type was evident regardless of whether the data were averaged over the entire deliberation period, or when time (.025-s bins) was involved, either as an additional classier feature or to construct the time courses of classification performance. The advantage for oscillatory activity, although notably not always significant by direct comparison with the ERP-based results, could be attributed to a number of factors. On the more interesting side, these might include the inherent insensitivity of ERPs to higher-frequency and non-phase-locked neural activity (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006; also see Solomon et al., 2017), but it is also difficult to rule out the fact that better classifier performance might merely be due to the increased number of features (i.e., the amount of information) available in the oscillatory data.

The second set of results from the EEG analyses providing further characterization of the differences between forward and backward recall notably demonstrated that the effects were transient as well as restricted in terms of frequency signature. That is, in analyzing the time course of classification, above-chance accuracy was not sustained throughout the deliberation period but was instead present at just two short latency clusters, beginning at about .7 and 2.3 seconds following cue onset and lasting around .1 second in each case (see Figure 5b). Additionally, analyses localizing activity simultaneously across both time and frequency further confirmed the reliability of the late effect, with accuracy exceeding chance across portions of both the low-and high-gamma bands (from around 50-100 Hz; see Figure 6b). The current results thus extend those of recent studies that have examined oscillatory signatures of retrieval accuracy in free recall. In particular, increases in posteriorlymaximal gamma power have been previously shown during the deliberation period leading up to successful recall (compared to intrusions) with both scalp EEG (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024) and intracranial EEG (e.g., Burke et al., 2014; Sederberg et al., 2007; Long et al., 2017). Together, these findings suggest that such high-frequency activity might be predominantly related to forward transitions (which, as we have discussed, are more frequent in free recall) and potentially modulated further by the direction of retrieval. We note, however, that any relationship between the role of gamma-band activity for our directional manipulation and that for retrieval success is only speculative and should await examination of both effects in the same experimental paradigm.

As noted in the Introduction (see section 1.), Katerman et al. (2022) also demonstrated an increase in theta power alongside a decrease in alpha power associated with free recall, with Li et al. (2024) subsequently confirming the alpha suppression effect with MVPA of scalp EEG. Distinct from those prior findings is the absence of such effects in the current study, which might be attributable to any number of differences or limitations of our design and analyses. For instance, we were unable to contrast neural activity according to recall accuracy, given that both intrusions and recalls in the uncued (incorrect) direction were relatively rare (combined, about a third as likely correct recalls). This leaves open the possibility that, although there is some discrepancy in the literature relating theta power increases versus decreases to episodic memory (e.g., Long and Kuhl, 2019; Osipova et al., 2006; for review, see Herweg et al., 2020), increases in theta might be more sensitive to successful retrieval or a mechanism that correlates with it, such as binding or reactivation (for reviews, see Hanslmayr et al., 2012; Nyhus and Curran, 2010). As the current results indicate, activity in the theta band might not be related to retrieval direction, especially when accuracy is equated across direction. Additionally, under the assumption that decreased alpha power is often correlated with task engagement or readiness (Griffiths et al., 2021; ; Hanslmayr et al., 2007; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996; also see Klimesch, 1997), it is possible that the extended duration and fixed timing of our deliberation periods mitigated any trial-by-trial differences in engagement. By contrast, it could be argued that subjects exhibit larger fluctuations in states of alertness or readiness in tasks such as free recall (and even recognition), where items might be self-generated (or tested) more rapidly and with more variation in retrieval success. Finally, while the extended (5-second) period prior to recall report in our task was designed to allow for continuous retrieval deliberation, and ideally isolate it from other cognitive processes, analogous to methods that have been successfully employed with MVPA in studies of working memory (e.g., Ester et al., 2015; LaRocque et al., 2013; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012), the free recall studies of Katerman et al. (2022) and Li et al. (2024) analyzed much shorter periods of about one second or less. Our long deliberation period thus might have included differential processing for forward vs. backward retrieval, but it was present in a transient or unpredictable manner, therefore weakening our ability to detect some of the difference. An obvious next step would be to shorten the deliberation period while still ensuring the minimization of artifact in the EEG due to verbal report.

In terms of further interpreting the neural differences observed here between forward and backward retrieval, it is potentially helpful to turn to one of the largely-invariant characteristics of the CRP: forward asymmetry. Even simple chaining models of memory have addressed this effect, positing that associations are formed between successive items in a list, and that forward associations are typically stronger than backward ones (Murdock, 1993; Raskin and Cook, 1937; Solway et al., 2012). Similarly, our results could reflect this difference in associative strength according to direction or, perhaps secondarily, subjects' attempts to overcome the difficulty with backward associations during the deliberation period (but notably doing so as to give rise to equivalent performance with forward retrieval by the end of the period). More recently, memory models that incorporate context as a central feature, such as the retrieved context theory (Howard and Kahana, 2002; for review, see Kahana, 2020), have proposed that the temporal contiguity effect occurs not only due to item-item associations but also as a result of an automatic process of forming reciprocal bonds between items and their presentation context. The forward asymmetry, as a result, can then be attributed to the encoding of a particular item based on the context created by just-presented items, which would not occur as strongly in the opposite (backward) direction. The effects we observed in the gamma band could thus reflect cortical activity associated with differences in hippocampally-mediated contextual reinstatement-an interpretation consistent with the memoryrelated interactions that have been observed between theta and gamma oscillations (e.g., Düzel et al., 2003; Koster et al., 2014; Mormann et al., 2005) and which might contribute to the ordering of episodic memories (Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Lisman, 2005; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; also see Nyhus and Curran, 2010). As we noted above, though, contrary to this account is our failure to observe theta differences, possibly due to these effects being limited to deep structures like the hippocampus and difficult to detect with scalp measures.

Considering the broader implications of our findings, there is a growing body of research contrasting the retrieval of past events and the simulation (or imagination) of future events (for reviews, see Schacter et al., 2012; Addis, 2020) to further understand the theoretical concept of mental time travel (MTT; Tulving, 1985 Tulving, , 2002)). Moreover, a subset of those studies has investigated the past and future at a more specific, or granular, level, which might be more analogous to the inter-item transitions we tested in the current study. For instance, Arzy et al. (2008 Arzy et al. ( , 2009) ) had subjects project themselves to different landmark time points in the past or future (i.e., 10 years in either direction) and then decide whether a particular personal or historical event had already occurred or was yet to happen. By setting such landmarks, a distinction could be made between absolute (past versus future) and relative (before or after the landmark) MTT. In addition to observing better behavioral performance (faster RTs and higher accuracy) for events nearer to compared to more distant from the present (also see Addis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007), performance was better in the relative future (i.e., forward) than the relative past (i.e., backward) direction. On the surface, those findings appear consistent with the forward asymmetry commonly observed in list memory studies but successfully mitigated by the procedure of the current study. Perhaps more interesting, however, are the scalp EEG correlates observed by Arzy et al. (2008), in which effects localized to lateral temporal and inferior frontal and parietal scalp were engaged for shorter durations in the relative future compared to relative past events. Despite the confound in difficulty, these results again leave open the possibility that directional retrieval engages distinct processing, consistent with the numerous behavioral findings from serial, free, and cued recall (as outlined in the Introduction). A beneficial path for future research would be to bring together the granular, item-based transitions involved in list memory with the longer-term transitions of personal and real-world events (which were on the order of years in Arzy et al., 2008 Arzy et al., , 2009)).

To conclude, the findings presented here extend those of recent studies using scalp EEG to understand the neural activity preceding successful memory recall (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024) and provide further evidence that retrieval processing is guided by temporal organization. Specifically, using a procedure that explicitly cued subjects to move either forward or backward over a memory list, we were able to not only replicate classic effects of serial position and recall contiguity but also equate behavioral performance across conditions. In doing so, the distinct patterns of high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory activity observed for forward and backward retrieval can confidently be attributed to deliberation and search processes engaged differently according to temporal direction, as opposed to other confounding factors (e.g., difficulty or retrieval outcome). Although a single study certainly comes with limitations, the novel design and analysis approach we describe here provides a possible starting point for understanding addressing how we mentally travel across immediate sequences as well as distant periods of our past and how scale-invariant temporal processes might serve episodic memory (Brown et al., 2007; Howard et al., 2015) Instances of AUC that are significantly greater than chance (dashed line at .5) are denoted by asterisks (*p < .025, **p < .01, one-tailed).
